title: H4 – Merit, signals and bias in selection
source: Zusammenfassung von Session 2 (Meritocracy, „Spoiled for choice“) und Session 3 „Recruitment and selection part 2“

blocks.text: Meritocracy promises rewards for talent and effort (IQ + Effort = Merit). But what looks like merit on a CV is partly produced by social class origins – economic, social and cultural capital (Bourdieu; Ingram, 2021).

Recruiters rely on signals (degrees, programmes) because they are expensive, granted by screening institutions and imply knowledge (Baron & Kreps, 1999) – but signals can be biased. The HR challenge is to distinguish the signal from the underlying job-relevant capability.
The search for cultural fit can reproduce inequality, depending on how fit is defined and assessed.
Inequality (outcomes), discrimination (treatment) and bias (cognition) are related but not interchangeable.
Field experiments (Quillian et al., 2019) show discrimination causally: equivalent applicants, only the ethnic cue varies.
Reducing bias and increasing diversity matters for fairness and for innovation (Mohammadi et al., 2017).
Bourdieu's capitals
Signaling theory (Baron & Kreps, 1999)
children: Expensive to obtain · granted by screening institutions · require knowledge
But: weight a signal by how it was produced

blocks.text: Biases (Weston & Woods, Box 6.1)
Unconscious bias in design
children: Standardized methods screen out neurodiverse people (Austin & Pisano, 2017)

blocks.text: Field experiments (Quillian et al., 2019)
children: Discrimination ratio = callback rate of white natives / callback rate of target group
France highest relative to the US (≈ 1.43), Germany lowest (≈ 0.92)

blocks.text: Diversity and innovation (Mohammadi et al., 2017)
children: Ethnic and disciplinary diversity → more innovation
Disciplinary diversity substitutable by external collaboration, ethnic diversity not

blocks.text: Core ideas of R&S
children: Carefully design the process: systematic & transparent criteria, validity/reliability/practicability, question signals and preconceptions
Involve a variety of actors: reduce unconscious bias, increase diversity

blocks.text: Read the CVs through Bourdieu: which capitals produced each signal, and which capabilities does the less-polished candidate show (work experience, responsibility, resilience)?
Name the biases in the decision-maker's reasoning and match each with a remedy (structured interviews, scoring rubrics set in advance, diverse panels, anonymised screening, work samples).
Be precise with concepts: an outcome gap is inequality; proving discrimination needs a design like a field experiment.
Make the case for change with two arguments: fairness and performance (innovation).
A system in which rewards, power and privilege are allocated by individual merit (talent and effort), not by social background.
Financial resources / resources from networks and group membership / knowledge, skills, education and expectations that give higher social standing (Bourdieu).
An observable credential (degree, training programme) used to infer unobservable ability (Baron & Kreps, 1999).
Unequal outcomes between groups.
Differential treatment associated with group membership.
A cognitive or attitudinal process that distorts judgement.
Callback rate of the majority group divided by the callback rate of the target group (Quillian et al., 2019).
Spoiled for choice: what skills might Peter have acquired that John did not – and why might a prestige-oriented CV screen undervalue them?
Why can't comparing real applicants show discrimination, while a field experiment can? (Causal inference.)
